extracted.intended_audience: general public, policy researchers, legal practitioners, industry stakeholders and activists seeking an overview of the FDA citizen petition process
extracted.subtask_description: Understanding and preparing FDA citizen petitions: who may file, what may be requested, the statutory/regulatory basis, timing requirements, and common uses/misuses (particularly in the pharmaceutical/ANDA context).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility to petition ("interested person")
rubrics_metrics.description: At any time, any "interested person" can request that the FDA "issue, amend, or revoke a regulation or order," or "take or refrain from taking any other form of administrative action." The process is available to individuals and community organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page emphasizes that citizen petitions are part of the basic law governing FDA actions and that the right to petition is broadly available (examples given: individuals, community organizations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of permissible requests
rubrics_metrics.description: Citizen petitions may ask the FDA to issue, amend, or revoke regulations or orders, or to take or refrain from taking other forms of administrative action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This wording defines the kinds of relief a petition can seek and frames petitions as a way to request regulatory or administrative changes from the FDA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory basis: 21 CFR Part 10
rubrics_metrics.description: The citizen petition process is described in Title 21 of the Code of Federal Regulations (21 CFR Part 10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should consult 21 CFR Part 10 for the regulatory text and procedural requirements governing petitions (the article links to the CFR section).

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 505(q) limitation on delaying ANDA approvals
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 505(q) (added in 2007) states that the FDA could not delay approving an ANDA due to concerns raised in a citizen petition unless the delay was "necessary to protect public health issues."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a statutory limitation on the effect a petition can have on generic drug approvals; it was enacted to reduce misuse of petitions to indefinitely delay generics.

rubrics_metrics.name: FDA response deadline for petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 505(q) originally mandated that the FDA respond to a petition within 180 days; this was shortened to 150 days via a 2011 amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior to these statutory deadlines there was no required FDA response time, which led to significant delays in approving generics. Timeliness is therefore a statutory criterion for FDA handling of petitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: FDA guidance to industry on petitions (2014)
rubrics_metrics.description: In 2014, the FDA issued guidance to industry about submitting citizen petitions and how it would consider them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guidance provides procedural expectations and instructions for petitioners; the article references that guidance as part of the current procedural framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common/strategic uses — challenging ANDA acceptance
rubrics_metrics.description: Innovator companies may present arguments to the FDA that an Abbreviated New Drug Application (ANDA) should not be accepted by filing a "citizen petition."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes this strategic use by brand companies as a mechanism to influence ANDA review and acceptance, illustrating one substantive target of petitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential for anti‑competitive or abusive use
rubrics_metrics.description: Pharmaceutical companies routinely use FDA citizen petitions to delay the entry of generic drugs into the United States marketplace; petitions have been criticized as a means to delay competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites empirical and policy literature documenting abuse (e.g., industry use to delay generics), notes that PhRMA sought changes in 2016 which the FDA declined, and situates statutory changes (505(q)) and FDA guidance as responses to such concerns.
